content: The Kaiser Richmond Field Hospital was the first hospital established by Kaiser Permanente and holds historical significance as a resource for the city of Richmond, California. It is also part of the Rosie the Riveter/World War II Home Front National Historical Park and is listed on the National Register of Historic Places. This hospital provided medical services to the surrounding communities until 1995, when it was replaced by the Richmond Medical Center, a modern facility located in downtown Richmond. The original field hospital, now closed, remains at its original site in South Richmond along Cutting Boulevard. During World War II, more American workers lost their lives in industrial accidents on the home front than U.S. soldiers who died in combat, at least until the Battle of Normandy in June 1944. In 2007, preliminary bus tours were introduced in Richmond, featuring a unique format where local residents shared their personal experiences from the wartime era, offering a deeper historical perspective on the area. Henry J. Kaiser, the owner of the Richmond Shipyards, recognized that maintaining a healthy workforce was essential to meeting the demanding construction deadlines of wartime America. He implemented a groundbreaking concept: pre-paid medical care for workers. This initiative soon expanded beyond the workforce and marked the first time many workers had access to medical care. The Kaiser Richmond Field Hospital, specifically built for the Richmond Shipyards, was funded by the U.S. Maritime Commission and opened on August 10, 1942. It was sponsored by Kaiser’s Permanente Foundation and operated under the leadership of Medical Director Dr. Sidney R. Garfield. The hospital was part of a three-tiered medical care system. This system included six well-equipped first aid stations located at individual shipyards and the Permanente Hospital in Oakland, which handled the most critical cases. Together, these facilities served employees of the Kaiser Shipyards who were enrolled in the Permanente Health Plan, commonly referred to as the Kaiser Plan. This plan was one of the first voluntary pre-paid medical plans in the United States and a direct precursor to modern health maintenance organizations (HMOs) as defined by the federal HMO Act of 1973. By August 1944, 92.2% of Richmond shipyard employees had joined the plan, making it the first voluntary group plan in the country to combine group medical practice, prepayment, and substantial medical facilities on such a large scale. After the war, the health plan was expanded to include workers’ families. By 1990, Kaiser Permanente had become the largest nonprofit HMO in the United States. Due to wartime material rationing, the field hospital was constructed as a single-story wood-frame building with a simple modernist design. Initially intended as an emergency facility, it opened with only 10 beds. However, later expansions increased its capacity to 160 beds by 1944. Kaiser Permanente also conducted its first medical research at the Richmond Field Hospital in 1942. This research later moved to another site, and by 1958, the organization had shifted its focus from animal research to correlational studies. The site of the field hospital, officially known as the Nystrom Tract Addition, is now owned by Masjeed Al-Noor. According to Martha Lee, National Park Superintendent, the Kaiser Richmond Field Hospital was the center of the nation’s first prepaid health care system and a precursor of today’s HMOs.
